items.t: Pfizer's 5.9% Yield vs. AbbVie's 53-Year Dividend Streak: Which Stock Is the Better Buy?
sum: Pfizer (PFE +0.21%) and AbbVie (ABBV +0.20%) rank among the biggest drugmakers in the world. Both pharma stocks have also been favorites for many income investors through the years.

However, Pfizer and AbbVie offer distinctly different attractions for income investors these days. Pfizer's 5.9% dividend yield is one of the highest in the healthcare sector. AbbVie's 2.5% yield isn't as eye-catching, but the company has increased its dividend for an impressive 53 consecutive years. Which of these stocks is the better pick right now?

It's obvious what Pfizer's main argument is: the mouthwatering yield. An investor who bought $10,000 of Pfizer stock would receive nearly $600 per year, compared to only around $250 from investing the same amount in AbbVie.

But is Pfizer's dividend safe? The company's payout ratio of roughly 246% could alarm some investors. However, that ratio is based on Pfizer's GAAP earnings, which include some one-time items such as acquisition-related costs that muddy the waters.

A better metric for assessing Pfizer's dividend safety is its free cash flow payout ratio. That number currently stands at 89%. Granted, Pfizer doesn't have much wiggle room at this level, but it's much more reassuring than the GAAP earnings-based payout ratio.

Importantly, Pfizer's management is adamant that no dividend cuts are forthcoming despite the company facing a patent cliff over the next couple of years. CFO Cecile Guegan said in the company's third-quarter earnings call, "So through the LOE [loss of exclusivity] period, our operating cash flow, financial assets, and access to capital markets will give us the ability to continue to invest and maintain the dividend."

The patent cliff will negatively impact Pfizer's revenue and earnings growth, though. Still, the company thinks that its newer products and late-stage pipeline candidates will help it return to growth later this decade.

Pfizer Just Raised Its 2026 Revenue Forecast by $1.5 Billion. Is the High-Yield Stock a Buy Right Now?
sum: Pfizer (PFE +0.21%) has a huge 5.8% dividend yield. That compares to roughly 1% for the broader market and 1.3% for the average pharmaceutical stock. Pfizer's shares have fallen 50% from their 2021 high, even after rallying over 15% so far in 2026. That said, the company just increased its full-year 2026 revenue guidance by $1.5 billion, which could be a sign for more aggressive investors to jump on board. But risk-averse investors may want to wait a little longer; here's why.

Pfizer traces its founding back to the mid-1800s. It has a proven history of success and is one of the most respected pharmaceutical companies on the planet. It was one of the few companies that quickly developed a COVID vaccine during the coronavirus pandemic, highlighting its technological capabilities. Given enough time, Pfizer is highly likely to get back on track as a business. This makes the current price attractive for risk-tolerant long-term investors.

But the company is facing headwinds, which is why the stock has fallen so far and offers such a high yield. In fact, the stock is back below its level prior to the development of a COVID vaccine. This is a key part of the story, since the stock rose dramatically during the pandemic. The outsize profits from that period, thanks to the vaccine, have ended. And the company is now facing several large patent cliffs, with Eliquis expected to face generic competition in 2028 and Vyndamax in 2031.

Meanwhile, Pfizer had to drop a GLP-1 weight-loss drug it was working on in 2025. That was a black eye for the company and left it without a product in a highly attractive new product category. It pivoted quickly, buying a company with a more attractive GLP-1 pipeline before 2025 was over. But investor sentiment was severely damaged, and as of this writing, the company still hasn't secured approval for a GLP-1 drug.

The point of that list of negatives is to show that Pfizer has been dealing with problems, and they aren't over yet. The stock price is where it is, pushing the yield to an elevated level, for a reason. More conservative investors may want to wait for further progress in drug development before buying this giant healthcare stock. However, if you can handle a little uncertainty, it may be worth taking the risk.

items.t: Blackstone Backs Pfizer's Obesity Bet as Analysts Turn More Bullish
sum: Pfizer has lined up outside capital for one of its most closely watched pipeline candidates. The drugmaker and Blackstone Life Sciences struck a deal to fund development of berobenatide, an experimental obesity treatment, with Blackstone-managed funds set to cover as much as $1.5 billion in development costs through 2028.

In return, Pfizer said Blackstone stands to collect milestone-linked payments tied to regulatory approval and commercial targets. The arrangement covers a medicine still under review rather than an approved product, leaving the payoff contingent on clinical and regulatory success. Investors greeted the news with a measured lift: Pfizer shares gained 1.0% and closed at €26.55.

The financing comes as Pfizer keeps spending on its own manufacturing footprint. On November 5 the company said it would commit $650 million over five years to a new Manufacturing Technology Center in Groton, Connecticut. The 220,000-square-foot site is designed to produce active ingredients and medicines for clinical trials, with construction expected to begin in the second quarter of 2027.

Pfizer's third-quarter 2026 results, released November 3, gave analysts something to work with. Revenue came in at $16.6 billion, while adjusted diluted earnings per share reached $0.87. On an operational basis, sales were broadly flat year over year. Reuters pointed to robust demand for Padcev and Eliquis as the main drivers.
Management lifted its full-year 2026 revenue forecast to a range of $62.0 billion to $64.0 billion, and now expects adjusted diluted EPS of $2.95 to $3.05 for the same period.

Freedom Broker responded on Friday by raising its price target to $34 from $33, according to media reports, while keeping its buy rating. Guggenheim had already moved a day earlier, lifting its target to $33 from $31 and likewise maintaining a buy recommendation. Neither firm changed its rating alongside the higher targets.

Clinical news has added to the momentum. On October 27 Pfizer reported positive phase 3 results from the MagnetisMM-32 study of ELREXFIO in patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma following treatment with an anti-CD38 therapy and lenalidomide.

sum: Pfizer has raised its sights for the full year after a third-quarter performance that came in well ahead of what the market had been expecting. The pharmaceutical giant now projects 2026 revenue of $62.0bn to $64.0bn, with adjusted diluted earnings per share of $2.95 to $3.05 — both ranges lifted alongside the quarterly release roughly a week ago.

The numbers behind that upgrade were solid. Revenue for the third quarter of 2026 reached $16.58bn, comfortably above the $15.85bn consensus tracked by FactSet. Adjusted diluted EPS came in at $0.87. Reuters attributed the momentum to robust demand for Eliquis and for Padcev, the cancer drug Pfizer picked up through acquisition.

Opinion on the stock is not unanimous. DZ Bank reportedly cut its rating from Buy to Hold on Friday while setting a $33 price target. Freedom Broker moved the other way on the same day, lifting its target from $33 to $34 and reaffirming its Buy call. The two houses thus find themselves on opposite sides of the fence: one has withdrawn its previous bullish stance, the other has kept the faith.

Investor attention now turns to November 17, 2026, when chief executive Albert Bourla will appear at the Jefferies London Healthcare Conference. Pfizer has announced a public webcast of the discussion, scheduled to begin at 9:00 GMT, with both audio and video available to shareholders and the wider public. Registration details were expected to be made available starting today.
On the corporate side, Pfizer confirmed on November 3 the appointment of Cecile Guegan as chief financial officer and executive vice president, effective November 1. She succeeds Dave Denton.

The company has also been busy on the research front. Edison Scientific announced an agreement with Pfizer on October 29 to deploy its AI platform, along with Kosmos, across Pfizer's biopharmaceutical R&D pipeline. About two weeks earlier, Pfizer reported a phase 3 win for ELREXFIO in the MagnetisMM-32 study, which met its primary endpoint on progression-free survival versus investigator's choice of standard therapies in patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma. And on October 26, the FDA broadened the approval of TALZENNA in combination with XTANDI to cover metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer harbouring mutations in HRR genes.

Pfizer (NYSE:PFE) Q3 2026: Guidance Raised on New Products
sum: - Launched and acquired products offset falling COVID sales.

Pfizer Inc. (NYSE:PFE) Healthcare Pfizer Inc (NYSE:PFE) 29.22 USD -0.010 0.034% Last Updated at: 2026-11-10T17:49:00Z has spent the past few years answering one question: what replaces the enormous revenue its COVID-19 products once generated? Its third-quarter 2026 report offered one of its most convincing answers yet. The New York-based drugmaker beat analyst forecasts for revenue and adjusted earnings and raised its full-year guidance for both, citing strong growth from launched and acquired products. For readers who follow Bluechip Stocks, the report highlights how a pharmaceutical giant is rebuilding growth while maintaining the scale and dividend that define a blue-chip stock.

Total revenue was relatively flat compared with the prior-year quarter on an operational basis. That headline masks two very different trends. Excluding contributions from Comirnaty and Paxlovid, its COVID vaccine and antiviral, revenue grew on an operational basis. Revenue from launched and acquired products grew strongly, more than offsetting sharp declines in the COVID franchise.

Adjusted diluted earnings per share beat analyst estimates by a wide margin. Reported diluted earnings per share fell compared with the prior year, partly because of a one-time charge tied to an in-licensing and collaboration agreement with Innovent Biologics, a Chinese biotechnology company. Adjusted gross margin and adjusted operating margin remained healthy.

Padcev, a cancer treatment acquired through the Seagen deal, grew strongly. Eliquis, the blood thinner Pfizer shares with Bristol Myers Squibb, the Vyndaqel family for a rare heart condition, Nurtec for migraine and Lorbrena for lung cancer also contributed. On the other side, Comirnaty and Paxlovid declined steeply, and the Prevnar pneumococcal vaccine family also declined in the quarter.

Pfizer raised its 2026 revenue guidance range and its adjusted earnings per share range. The new earnings range already absorbs the one-time Innovent charge. Management attributed the higher outlook to stronger year-to-date performance, accelerating contributions from newer products and progress on cost improvement initiatives.

What Happens To Pfizer Stock If Patent Losses Outpace New Drugs?
sum: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

Pfizer (PFE) stock yields 5.8%, paying holders to wait while the company replaces its older drugs. During its November 3, 2026 call, management named the loss of exclusive rights to Ibrance and Xtandi in the U.S., and to Eliquis outside it, as a key factor for 2027. Management provided only high-level drivers for 2027, and the worry is that those losses arrive faster than the newer drugs grow. So how close are those losses to showing up in Pfizer’s sales?

Management placed the losses in 2027, and current sales are close to flat. Pfizer posted quarterly revenue of $16.6 billion in fiscal Q3 2026, compared to $16.7 billion a year earlier, as lower sales of COVID-19 products offset growth in non-COVID products. On November 3, management raised the midpoint of its 2026 revenue guide from $61.5 billion to $63 billion.

Management already expects the patent losses to weigh on the balance sheet. Leverage, its debt measured against earnings, should stay around current levels or rise modestly while the patents run out, management said. Pfizer’s 2026 guidance includes no share buybacks.

Over the twelve months to September 27, 2026, Pfizer generated $11.8 billion in free cash flow, the cash left after capital spending, compared to $9.79 billion paid in dividends. So the patent losses would have to cut free cash flow by about $2.0 billion a year before the business stopped covering its dividend from the cash it brings in.

That makes the risk mainly one for the dividend, not for Pfizer’s ability to pay its debts. Over the same twelve months, operating income covered interest expense 6.1 times. The share price is a separate risk. During the 2023 bond yield shock, from July 25 to December 13, 2023, Pfizer fell 26%, while the S&P 500 lost 9.5%.

Pfizer has newer drugs growing against the losses. Led by Padcev, its launched and acquired products brought in $3.8 billion in fiscal Q3 2026, up 32% by management’s measure. Management said it keeps investing behind these products to offset the patent losses over the next several years. Management also expects to deliver nearly all of $7.2 billion in net cost savings by the end of 2026, and it plans another $2.5 billion from 2027 through 2029.

The stock's reception has been cool. Shares slipped 1.1% on Friday to close at €26.34, with media coverage pointing to softer sales of COVID products as the drag. That tepid reaction sits alongside the raised guidance Pfizer issued just over a week ago — a forecast that now serves as the yardstick for coming quarterly reports.

Pfizer reported third-quarter 2026 revenue of $16.6 billion on Tuesday, with adjusted diluted earnings per share of $0.87. Those figures form the financial starting point against which the pipeline story will be measured.

For the full year 2026, the company expects revenue of $62.0 billion to $64.0 billion and adjusted diluted EPS of $2.95 to $3.05. Hitting those numbers with the existing business — and backing them up with progress in the drug portfolio — is what matters from here, and oncology offers a concrete test given that both clinical and regulatory advances are already in hand.

Pfizer said on October 27 that ELREXFIO met the primary endpoint on progression-free survival in the Phase 3 MagnetisMM-32 trial, which enrolled patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma. The company plans to submit the data to regulators worldwide. The upside case rests on those filings going ahead and translating into regulatory decisions that could improve the drug's commercial prospects.

TALZENNA is further along. The FDA on October 26 approved it in combination with XTANDI for an earlier treatment setting in metastatic prostate cancer, covering adults with certain HRR gene mutations. That opens an additional option within a clearly defined patient group — value that depends on how successfully Pfizer commercializes the expanded label.

Alongside the quarterly numbers, Pfizer named Cecile Guegan as chief financial officer effective November 1, disclosing the decision Tuesday in a mandatory filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission.

sum: Two research houses landed on an identical $33 price target for Pfizer this week and still walked away with opposite recommendations. DZ Bank downgraded the stock from Buy to Hold, according to media reports, while Guggenheim lifted its target from $31 to $33 and kept its Buy rating. The divergence came just days after the drugmaker published third-quarter 2026 results and raised its full-year outlook.
The shares slipped 1.1% in the session following the DZ Bank move.

Pfizer reported revenue of $16.583 billion for the three months, alongside an adjusted diluted loss per share of $0.87. On a reported basis, earnings per share came in at $0.56. Management also lifted its 2026 revenue guidance to a range of $62.0 billion to $64.0 billion, and now expects adjusted diluted earnings per share of $2.95 to $3.05.

Those upgraded numbers cover both the topline and the adjusted bottom line. Whether they translate into a durable growth story is the question now dividing the analyst community. Flat overall sales and a continuing decline in COVID-related products sat alongside the brighter profit forecast — a combination that leaves the bull case resting on whether newer medicines can offset that drag.

Pfizer has been stacking up clinical and regulatory wins in quick succession. On October 27, the company said ELREXFIO hit the primary endpoint of the Phase 3 MagnetisMM-32 trial, which evaluated the drug against physician's choice of standard therapies in patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma. The endpoint was progression-free survival, and Pfizer intends to file the data with health authorities worldwide — a potential regulatory catalyst if those submissions go ahead and the reviews come back positive.

A day earlier, the company announced FDA approval for TALZENNA in combination with XTANDI for earlier use in metastatic prostate cancer. Progress also came on the pediatric pneumococcal vaccine front on October 24, when Phase 2 results showed immune responses against all serotypes studied. Safety and tolerability were comparable to Prevnar 20, according to the company, and the findings support the ongoing Phase 3 program.

sum: Pfizer Limited reported stronger quarterly sales in India on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, while a one-time payment linked to Minipress XL significantly lifted reported profit. According to Kotak Neo, revenue from operations reached 726.86 crore Indian rupees in the September quarter, up 13.2 percent from a year earlier.

Net profit rose 65.7 percent to 313.25 crore Indian rupees. The result included an exceptional gain of 132.06 crore rupees after Pfizer Inc. decided to discontinue manufacturing Minipress XL in the United States from September 7, 2026. Pfizer Limited is to receive a lump-sum payment connected with the end of its marketing, distribution and sale of the medicine in India.

The underlying picture was firmer but less dramatic. Profit before tax and exceptional items increased 13.9 percent to 290.77 crore rupees, while earnings per share before the exceptional item rose to 47.09 rupees from 41.32 rupees in the year-earlier quarter. The distinction matters for investors because the payment raises the reported result without creating a recurring earnings stream.

For the six months ended September 2026, revenue from operations increased 10.8 percent to 1,380.03 crore rupees. Profit before exceptional items and tax grew 10.2 percent to 567.45 crore rupees, while reported net profit reached 517.72 crore rupees after including the September-quarter gain.

Operating cash generation for the first half was 358.99 crore rupees, down from 599.47 crore rupees a year earlier. Pfizer Limited also paid its final dividend of 75 rupees per share for fiscal 2026 on August 4, 2026, after shareholder approval.

Pfizer Limited says it operates more than 150 products across 15 therapeutic areas and four key business categories in India. Its activities include local manufacturing and the supply of medicines, with quality controls covering production. The company operates in the branded-pharmaceutical and vaccine market alongside larger Indian drugmakers such as Sun Pharmaceutical Industries, Cipla and Abbott India, while Pfizer remains a multinational affiliate focused on selected global brands and therapeutic areas.
India's pharmaceutical shares remain sensitive to product launches, pricing regulation and the quality of reported earnings.

Missed Out On Pfizer's Run? Here Is What Holders Saw
sum: If Pfizer sat on your watchlist instead of in your portfolio, the past few months may feel like a missed call. Holding Pfizer from the start of the year would have returned 28.6%, including dividends. That outcome followed fresh oncology approvals, obesity data and a new China-focused cancer partnership that grabbed headlines late in the period. Back on 1 January 2026, what confidence in Pfizer's aging-population and emerging-market earnings story could have justified acting sooner?
If the move has made Pfizer harder to judge, start where the gap is still open and scan 33 high quality undervalued stocks.
The shares cost US$24.9 at the start, and anyone looking at Pfizer then had to decide which earnings story felt more realistic.

The bullish narrative pointed to a Fair Value of US$37.92, essentially the price implied if aging populations and emerging markets fed through as expected. That view leaned on assumptions that revenue would decline only 0.9% a year while profit margins moved from 16.8% to 23.1% by 2028.

The bearish case anchored around a Fair Value of US$23.58, suggesting limited upside if regulatory pressure bit harder. This scenario assumed revenue would decline 4.2% annually, with losses of exclusivity on drugs like Eliquis and Ibrance creating a steep competitive and pricing hit.

The most concrete development for Pfizer was Q3 2026 results that showed revenue at US$16,583m and net income at US$3,242m, both lower than a year earlier, with net margin slipping from 21.3% to 19.6%. That challenged the bullish idea of improving profitability. New oncology approvals and obesity data supported the long-term growth angle, so the period cut both ways.

The real lesson is where to look first. When a thesis leans on margin expansion, track net margin and absolute profit in each report and test whether new approvals are shifting those numbers or just refreshing the story.

Why Pfizer (PFE) Stock Is Trading Up Today
sum: Shares of global pharmaceutical company Pfizer (NYSE:PFE) jumped 3.8% in the afternoon session after positive clinical trial results from peers Merck and Moderna for an mRNA cancer treatment lifted sentiment across the pharmaceutical sector.

The two companies reported that their mRNA cancer treatment met its primary goal in a Phase 3 clinical trial when combined with the drug Keytruda. This study, which included 1,137 patients, demonstrated a statistically significant improvement in recurrence-free survival compared to using Keytruda by itself.
The shares closed the day at $28.23, up 3.7% from the previous close.
Is now the time to buy Pfizer? Access our full analysis report here, it's free.

Pfizer's shares are not very volatile and have only had 3 moves greater than 5% over the last year. In that context, today's move indicates the market considers this news meaningful, although it might not be something that would fundamentally change its perception of the business.

The biggest move we wrote about over the last year was 11 months ago when the stock gained 7.2% on the news that the company announced a landmark agreement with the U.S. government aimed at lowering prescription drug prices for American patients.

The historic pact includes several key measures. Pfizer will voluntarily align prices for its drugs in Medicaid programs with those in other developed countries, a policy referred to as 'most-favored-nation' pricing.

items.t: Pfizer's 6.5% Dividend Yield Looked Too Good to Be True -- but Management Just Silenced the Skeptics
sum: The higher the dividend yield, the more investors tend to worry. Pfizer (PFE -0.20%) boasts a forward dividend yield of 6.5%, the highest yield among large-cap healthcare stocks. Unsurprisingly, some have viewed Pfizer as a yield trap.

While Pfizer's dividend yield may have looked too good to be true for some investors, that shouldn't be the case now. The company provided its first-quarter update on Tuesday, May 5, 2026. And I think that management just silenced the skeptics.

Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla addressed any doubts about the drugmaker's commitment to its dividend in the Q1 call, stating, "We intend to maintain and over time, grow our dividend as we continue to delever and build long-term value." CFO David Denton reinforced this message, saying that Pfizer's strategy includes "maintaining and over time growing our dividend."

Were those just meaningless words? I don't think so. One reason is that Pfizer now has greater cash flow visibility thanks to legal settlements related to the Vyndamax patent infringement and a Belgian court ruling on Comirnaty contracts with European Union countries. These two developments significantly improve Pfizer's ability to support its dividend.

Pfizer has made large acquisitions in the past that resulted in dividend cuts. Could history repeat itself? Bourla was asked about this possibility in the Q1 earnings call. He replied that Pfizer will always explore merger and acquisition opportunities, but the company isn't planning to pursue a large-scale merger. Bourla added that the disruption of a mega merger would negatively affect the organization's execution of its artificial intelligence (AI) transformation.

The near term looks good for Pfizer. The company generated more operating cash flow in Q1 than it needed to cover the dividend. Pfizer beat Wall Street's expectations with its Q1 results. Denton hinted that the drugmaker would probably have raised its guidance were it not for his "philosophy of not really adjusting in Q1."

The longer term looks bright, too. Management now has "greater confidence" that the company will deliver high single-digit revenue growth beginning in 2029. Pfizer's pipeline programs have promising prospects, especially its cancer and obesity therapies in development.

items.t: 3 Monster Dividend Stocks to Hold for the Next 10 Years
sum: Bob Dylan's lyrics that "the times, they are a-changin'" have never been truer. Artificial intelligence (AI) is disrupting businesses. The geopolitical world order is undergoing major upheaval. Populations are aging in many countries, including the U.S.
How can income investors best position their portfolios for this era of radical transition? Here are three monster dividend stocks to hold for the next 10 years.

In the midst of massive changes, at least one thing will remain constant: The world will need energy. And it's become increasingly clear that natural gas and natural gas liquids (NGLs) will remain critical components in meeting those energy needs. That's great news for Enterprise Products Partners LP (EPD -0.89%).

This limited partnership (LP) is one of my favorite pipeline stocks. Enterprise Products Partners operates over 50,000 miles of pipelines across the U.S. It also has other midstream energy assets, including 45 natural gas processing trains and over 300 million barrels of liquid storage facilities. Roughly 55% of Enterprise's gross operating margin stems from its NGL business, and 16% comes from its natural gas operations.

Income investors seek stability. Enterprise Products Partners delivers. The company has consistently generated dependable cash flow, even during tumultuous periods such as the financial crisis of 2007 through 2009 and the COVID-19 pandemic of 2020 through 2022.

Enterprise's forward distribution yield currently stands at almost 6%. The LP has increased its distribution for an impressive 27 consecutive years. I think it's in a great position to keep that streak going over the next decade.

An unfortunate reality with aging populations is that the demand for healthcare increases. As individuals age, they're more likely to be diagnosed with cancer and other serious diseases. Their immune systems become weaker, so vaccines are more critical. Pfizer (PFE -0.54%) is one of the top pharmaceutical companies poised to address these challenges.

Eli Lilly Soared by 39% in 2025, but Here's Another Healthcare Stock to Buy in 2026
sum: Eli Lilly's (LLY +1.46%) share price jumped 39% in 2025, driven by investors eager to benefit from the success of the company's GLP-1 drugs, Mounjaro (for diabetes) and Zepbound (for weight loss). That said, the company's position at the top of the GLP-1 heap isn't guaranteed, with Novo Nordisk (NVO -1.97%) beating Eli Lilly to market with a GLP-1 pill. If you are looking at Eli Lilly, you might want to consider a pharmaceutical stock like Pfizer (PFE +0.39%), which is relatively unloved right now, instead. Here's why.

The pharmaceutical sector is highly competitive and driven by innovation. GLP-1 weight loss drugs are a perfect example. Novo Nordisk was first to market with a GLP-1 shot. Eli Lilly's GLP-1 shots were better received by the market and quickly became the leading options. In early 2026, however, Novo Nordisk was first to market with a GLP-1 pill, which could give it a chance to win back market share. Eli Lilly plans to bring out its own pill, so Novo Nordisk's advantage could be short-lived.

That said, after a strong price advance driven by the excitement around GLP-1 drugs, Eli Lilly's valuation seems stretched. The stock's price-to-earnings ratio is a lofty 50. For comparison, the S&P 500 index, which is trading near all-time highs, has a P/E of 28. If valuation matters to you, you'll probably be better off with a competitor like Pfizer, which is relatively unloved.

Pfizer's internally developed GLP-1 drug didn't pan out and had to be abandoned. That's bad and helps explain why investors have been less than positive about the company's future, noting that its P/E ratio is just 15. However, Pfizer has a long and successful history in the drug sector. It may not be the most innovative company right now, but history suggests it will, eventually, develop new and exciting blockbuster drugs.

Notably, its GLP-1 setback was quickly followed up by the acquisition of a company with a promising GLP-1 pipeline and a partnership to distribute a Chinese company's GLP-1 pill if it is approved. In other words, Pfizer isn't giving up; it is adjusting just like it always has.
If you don't mind a turnaround story, Pfizer's relatively attractive valuation could be a much better option than richly priced Eli Lilly.

Pfizer shares slump 3.60% on fourth quarter loss, lower 2026 outlook
sum: Shares of US drugmaker Pfizer Inc. slumped on Tuesday following a fourth quarter loss due to a large write-down. It also forecast lower revenues for 2026.

The pharma giant highlighted another fall in quarterly revenues tied to Covid-19 products, and $4.4 billion in asset impairments that were needed "due to changes in development plans and updated long-range commercial forecasts," Pfizer said in a statement.

The results also indicated that the firm again plans no share buyback this year as it works to limit its debt while funding a research and development program intended to offset the hit from lost patent advantages.
"Current financial guidance does not anticipate any share repurchases in 2026," said Pfizer.
The company anticipates R&D expenses between $10.5 billion and $11.5 billion in 2026. In 2025, it spent $10.4 billion on R&D.
At 1:01 p.m. EST, Pfizer stock was down 3.60%, or $0.96, at $25.70.
The drugmaker reported a loss of $1.6 billion for October-December 2025 period when compared with $410 million profit in the fourth quarter of 2024.

Pfizer shares drop 5% with 2026 revenue projection and long-range outlook
sum: With COVID sales falling and patent protections expiring, Pfizer is forecasting its 2026 revenue to be in the range of $59.5 billion to $62.5 billion. The midpoint of the projection ($61 billion) would be a decline from this year’s estimated revenue of $62 billion—which the company reaffirmed on Tuesday. It would also be an additional slide from Pfizer’s 2024 revenue of $63.6 billion.

Built into the 2026 guidance is a $1.5 billion decline in sales of its COVID products—from an estimated $6.5 billion this year to $5 billion in expected sales next year. The company also expects to sustain a $1.5 billion hit from the loss of exclusivity (LOE) of its products.
As those LOEs escalate in the coming years—to $3 billion-plus in 2027 and $6-plus in 2028—the drugmaker said that it doesn’t expect to see growth until 2029.
With the updated guidance, Pfizer’s share price fell by 5% by mid-morning on Tuesday.

“Once 2028 is behind us, the vast majority of those LOEs are done and the growth drivers that we invest in over the next several years will be maintained and that should allow us to begin to accelerate the top line,” Pfizer chief financial officer Dave Denton said in a conference call.
As for its COVID products, Denton said that sales of its antiviral Paxlovid are tumbling at a higher rate than those for its mRNA vaccine.

“Paxlovid is more significantly affected as its utilization is directly related to infection rates of the COVID virus,” Denton said. “Comirnaty has shown a slower rate of decline as patients continue to seek protection from COVID via vaccinations despite the narrowing of government eligibility recommendations.”
